title: How HTTPS keeps your data private
performance: after the video, the viewer can explain in plain words how a browser and a site make a trip private before any data is sent (the site proves who it is, the two sides agree a secret key, then everything is scrambled), and can say what the padlock does and does not promise

audience.assumed_prior: uses the web, email and work apps daily; has seen the padlock and certificate warnings; knows public wifi is risky; has no networking background
audience.why: the brief's audience are working adults who rely on the padlock without knowing what it checks; the sheet defines seven plain terms and assumes only everyday browser use
audience.motivation: wants to avoid leaking a login or work data and to know when to trust what the browser shows; mildly uneasy that the padlock is a symbol they have never been shown
audience.context: desk or laptop at work, often with sound, captions on; first language varies, so screen words stay short and labels are single plain words

strategy.name: worked_example_led
strategy.rationale: the sheet is a sequence of steps in one handshake (identity check, shared key, scrambled data) that is best taught by running one login through it once, narrating each step; the brief asks for the same trip retold from open to private
strategy.signature_move: show the login on the open path, add the one protection for that moment, show what the watcher now sees, THEN name the part just used

misconceptions.belief: the padlock means the site is safe and honest
misconceptions.why_tempting: the icon looks like a security seal and sits next to the address, so it reads as a verdict on the site
misconceptions.source_anchor: F18, F19, not_claimed: the padlock means the site is safe, honest or trustworthy

misconceptions.belief: the secret key is simply sent across to the server, perhaps locked, and a watcher could grab it
misconceptions.why_tempting: sending a key over the same open network sounds like it must expose it
misconceptions.source_anchor: F12, F13 (the key is agreed without being sent readable; a watcher who sees the exchange cannot practically work it out)

hook.sketch: A login leaves a browser, crosses a shared network and reaches a server. On the way a watcher sits on the path, and the plain data reads like a postcard.

arc.promise: in about two minutes you will see how the same trip becomes private in three moves, and what the padlock really tells you
arc.bridge_from_prior: sec1 opens from the padlock and the certificate warning the viewer has already seen in their browser, set beside the trip the data actually takes

sections.goal: the viewer can explain how a browser uses a certificate to decide whether a server is who it claims, naming the three checks it makes
the viewer can explain why two sides can agree a shared secret key across an open network that a watcher who sees the whole exchange cannot practically work out
the viewer can use the three protections (identity, shared key, scrambled data with tamper detection) to judge what the padlock does and does not promise about a site

arc.payoff: Back to the opening login on the same shared network: the packets still pass the watcher, who now sees only noise; the padlock marks a private trip to the claimed site, and the viewer knows it says nothing about whether the site is honest.

practice_ladder.what: one login run through identity check, shared key and scrambled data, the watcher's view changing at each step
a different fictional site: the viewer picks which connection should carry a password and why a certificate from a trusted authority for a different name still fails
next time the browser shows a padlock or a warning, the viewer asks the two questions the lesson taught: is the name right, and is this only a private trip

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Issuer, name, date: three checks before a single byte of the login moves.

Two connections to a different fictional site. A: valid certificate for the exact address typed. B: certificate from a trusted authority, but made out for a different site name. Which would you let carry a password?
recall_moments.answer: A: the issuer, name and date checks all pass, so the trip is private to the site you asked for; B fails the name check, so the browser should warn
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: B looks fine because its issuer is trusted, but a trusted issuer is only one of three checks; the name must also match the address typed

transfer_tasks: the next time the browser shows a padlock or a certificate warning, check that the address is the one you meant and treat the padlock as a private trip, not as a verdict on the site

persona.voice: an analyst: precise, calm, a little dry; explains each step of the mechanism and says plainly what each part does and does not promise, speaking to a capable colleague
persona.delivery_notes: even and unhurried on the hook, slower and plain on the shared key, brisk on the quiz setup with a clear pause cue, level and exact on the padlock's limits; short sentences, no jargon without the picture on screen

gagne.attention: hook: the plain login crossing the shared network with a watcher reading it
gagne.objective: promise: the same trip private in three moves, and what the padlock really tells you
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 opens from the padlock and warning the viewer has already seen
gagne.present: sec1 to sec3 in dependency order: who the site is, then the shared key, then the scrambled trip and its limits
gagne.guidance: signature move on the one running login: add the protection, show the watcher's view, then name it
gagne.practice: quiz after sec3 on a different site; transfer task
gagne.feedback: the quiz answer explains why B (trusted issuer, wrong name) still fails
gagne.assess: the quiz is the final check
gagne.transfer: transfer task on the viewer's own browser; payoff returns to the opening login

merrill.problem_centered: one login crossing a shared network runs through the whole lesson
merrill.activation: sec1 bridges from the padlock and warnings the viewer has seen
merrill.demonstration: sec1 to sec3 run the login through each step with the watcher's view beside it
merrill.application: quiz on a different site; transfer task
merrill.integration: transfer task in the viewer's own browsing; payoff shows the same trip now private

mayer.coherence: one running login plus one quiz; no algorithm names, no versions, no side stories
mayer.signalling: the part being explained is the accent as it is spoken; one slowdown on the shared key
mayer.redundancy: screen shows single-word labels; narration carries the explanation; captions on
mayer.contiguity: each check, key and scramble appears as the narration names it
mayer.segmenting: three short sections, one move each, a recall prompt after the first
mayer.pre_training: the hook names the parts on screen (browser, server, watcher) before the handshake runs

arcs.attention: the readable login with a watcher in the hook
arcs.relevance: the viewer's own padlock and certificate warnings, and the transfer task
arcs.confidence: a full worked trip before the quiz asks anything
arcs.satisfaction: payoff: the same trip, watcher sees noise, padlock understood
